newsitem.title: ITALY: Italy's BNL, INA interested in Banco Napoli.
newsitem.headline: Italy's BNL, INA interested in Banco Napoli.

text.p: State-controlled Banca Nazionale del Lavoro said on Sunday it would join forces with insurer INA and declare a preliminary interest in the sale of loss-making Banco di Napoli.

The Italian Treasury, which holds a majority stake in BNL, has temporariliy taken control of the ailing Banco di Napoli and has promised to sell a 60 percent holding in southern Italy's largest bank by the end of the year.

It has given potential buyers until Monday to send a letter of interest in the offer. They will then be allowed to take a close look at Banco di Napoli books and if they like what they see, will have until December 20 to make a full bid.
But any move by BNL and INA would undoubtedly raise question marks about the credibility of Italy's privatisation programme.

BNL president Mario Sarcinelli told financial daily Il Sole 24 Ore that his bank was not yet making any commitments. "At this stage, all BNL is investing in Banco di Napoli is the cost of a postage stamp," he said.
However, if INA and BNL did decide to make a joint offer, Sarcinelli indicated that INA would provide much of the cash while his group would provide the know-how to run a bank.
INA, which is controlled by banks Istituto Bancario San Paolo Di Torino, IMI and Cariplo, has not commented on the joint initiative.
Only Banco Ambrosiano Veneto and Banca Commerciale Italiano have previously indictated they might be interested in Banco di Napoli, but both groups have now said no.

Banco di Napoli unveiled record losses of 3.12 trillion lire ($2.0 billion) in 1995 and plunged a further 674 billion lire into the red in the first half of this year thanks largely to a poor, highly politicised loan policy.
The Treasury has installed new management at the firm and has promised to take on the vast bulk of the company's huge stock of bad debt before selling the group.

The European Commission has indicated to the Treasury that it wants Banco di Napoli to be sold by year end. If the auction fails to attract a buyer, the government might be forced to break up the bank and try to sell its various units separately.
Treasury Minister Carlo Azeglio Ciampi is against this, but would run into flak if BNL took partial control of the group.
The Treasury controls over 70 percent of BNL and still exerts considerable influence over insurance firm INA, which was only fully privatised in June, sector analysts said.
"A privatisation...does not consist in the sale of a Treasury owned company to a Treasury controlled company," Il Sole 24 Ore wrote in an editorial on Sunday.
BNL's Sarcinelli has previously shown little interest in Banco di Napoli but denied that his bank had been told by its majority shareholder to show an interest in the sale.
"Why can't we ask to take a close look at Banco di Napoli books?" he said, adding: "We have had no pressure put on us."

However Italian newsagency AGI reported that not all BNL's shareholders were happy with developments. It said state national insurance body INPs, which holds around 11 percent of BNL's capital, had decided to oppose any possible bid.
Banco di Napoli savings shares, the only ones still being traded on the Milan bourse, surged over five percent on Friday to 589.4 lire on rumours of possible interest in the group. $1 = 1,517 lire
